title: Execution-Trace Guided Remasking for Diffusion Code Generation

raw.stage1:
**Purpose:**  
The purpose of the contribution is to provide semantic guidance to diffusion code models about where errors occur, instead of relying on confidence-based remasking heuristics. Paper [22] ("DynaFix: Iterative Automated Program Repair Driven by Execution-Level Dynamic Information") shares a substantively equivalent purpose, as it aims to improve automated program repair by incorporating dynamic execution-level information to guide the repair process. This aligns with the goal of using execution-based signals to guide error localization and repair.  

**Mechanism:**  
The mechanism involves an execution-trace-guided remasking pipeline that parses exception tracebacks or line-level execution traces from failing unit tests, maps failure-relevant lines to token indices, and remasks only those tokens for conditional diffusion repair. Paper [9] ("TraceFixer: Execution Trace-Driven Program Repair") uses execution traces to identify failure-relevant code lines and predict edits for program repair, which is substantively equivalent to the proposed mechanism of using execution traces to guide token remasking for repair.  

**Evaluation:**  
The evaluation design involves implementing the method as a three-stage inference-time algorithm (initial generation, execution-based localization, targeted conditional repair) and evaluating it on MBPP+. Paper [27] ("RepairBench: Leaderboard of Frontier Models for Program Repair") uses execution-based evaluation for program repair, compiling and executing patches to validate their correctness. This matches the evaluation design at the level of execution-based validation, even though the specific benchmark (MBPP+) differs.  

**Domain:**  
The domain is diffusion-based code generation and repair. Paper [4] ("CodeDiffuSe: A masked diffusion framework for structure-aware code completion and repair") operates in the same general application area of code generation and repair using diffusion models, making the domain covered.

## PURPOSE: Give diffusion code models semantic guidance about where errors occur instead of confidence-based remasking heuristics.

The purpose is specifically to replace confidence-based remasking in diffusion models with semantically-grounded (execution-trace-based) error localization. Papers [2], [3], [5], [6], [10] all address the problem of improving remasking in diffusion language models beyond confidence heuristics — they explicitly identify "confidence-based remasking is insufficient" as the gap. Paper [3] (RemeDi) states "The key challenge is to identify potential errors in the inputs" and proposes self-reflective remasking. Paper [5] (CORE) explicitly targets "static confidence scores" as myopic. Paper [2] (Corrective DLMs) states "inability to distinguish between correct and erroneous tokens." All share the same objective: better error localization for diffusion model remasking. However, none of these use execution traces as the semantic signal — they use model-internal signals. The PURPOSE at the problem-class level is "improve error localization for diffusion remasking beyond confidence heuristics," which IS covered by [2], [3], [5], [6].

## MECHANISM: Execution-trace guided remasking — parse exception tracebacks/line-level traces from failing unit tests, map failure-relevant lines to token indices, remask only those tokens for conditional diffusion repair.

The key primitive is: use program execution traces/tracebacks to localize which tokens to remask in a diffusion model. Paper [9] (TraceFixer) uses execution traces to guide program repair — "predicts how to edit source code so that it does not diverge from the desired behavior" using execution trace divergence. However, TraceFixer is not a diffusion model and doesn't do remasking. Paper [19] (EG-CFG) uses execution signals during code generation inference. Paper [22] (DynaFix) uses execution-level dynamic information iteratively for program repair. Paper [1] uses code diffusion for repair. None of the prior papers combine: (1) execution trace parsing → (2) token-index mapping → (3) selective remasking in a diffusion model. The closest is [9] for execution-trace-driven repair, but the specific primitive of mapping execution traces to token-level remask decisions in a diffusion model is not present. Paper [4] (CodeDiffuSe) does diffusion-based code repair but uses structure-aware masking, not execution traces. This combination appears genuinely absent.

## EVALUATION: Three-stage inference-time algorithm evaluated on MBPP+.

MBPP+ is a well-known code generation benchmark. Paper [1] evaluates code diffusion models on standard benchmarks. Paper [4] evaluates on code repair benchmarks. The evaluation design — running a code generation/repair system on MBPP+ and measuring pass rates — is a standard benchmark evaluation used across many code generation papers. MBPP/MBPP+ is used in papers like [19] and others in the code generation space. The evaluation design (benchmark-based pass@k evaluation on MBPP+) is a standard design covered by prior work.

## DOMAIN: Diffusion-based code generation and repair.

Papers [1], [4] explicitly work in diffusion-based code generation and repair. Paper [1]: "leverage pre-trained code diffusion models for the problem of last-mile repair." Paper [4]: "masked diffusion framework specifically designed" for code completion and repair. This domain is clearly covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to explain why semantic localization is essential for effective diffusion repair. Semantic localization refers to identifying specific program regions relevant to a fault and focusing repair efforts on those regions. This purpose is not directly covered by any prior paper. While papers like [16] ("Semantic Fault Localization for Mutation-based Program Repair") and [19] ("Diffusion is a code repair operator and generator") discuss fault localization and diffusion-based repair, neither explicitly establishes the necessity of semantic localization for diffusion repair effectiveness. They focus on techniques or applications rather than the empirical relationship between semantic localization and repair success.

### Mechanism
The contribution uses edit-distance analysis to compare code modifications made by trace-guided repair versus global low-confidence repair. Papers [2] ("Algorithm to Determine Extended Edit Distance between Program Codes"), [6] ("Theoretical Analysis of Edit Distance Algorithms"), [7] ("Revisiting Code Similarity Evaluation with Abstract Syntax Tree Edit Distance"), and [17] ("Basic Investigation of Code Edit Distance Measurement by CodeBERT") all involve edit-distance analysis in various forms. For example, [2] introduces an extended edit distance algorithm for program codes, and [7] applies AST-based edit distance for code similarity evaluation. These papers demonstrate substantively equivalent mechanisms for analyzing code modifications using edit distance, even if applied to different contexts.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design measures the effectiveness of trace-guided repair versus global low-confidence repair using metrics like mean edit distance and zero-edit fraction. Papers [2], [7], and [17] all use edit-distance-based metrics to evaluate code modifications, which matches the evaluation design. For instance, [7] uses AST edit distance to evaluate code similarity, and [17] uses CodeBERT to measure code edit distance. These prior works demonstrate the same evaluation design (edit-distance-based metrics), even though the specific objects of evaluation differ.

### Domain
The domain is repair behavior analysis, specifically analyzing how different repair strategies modify code. Papers like [3] ("Enhancing Program Repair with Specification Guidance and Intermediate Behavioral Signals"), [9] ("Semantic program repair using a reference implementation"), [15] ("Restore: Retrospective Fault Localization Enhancing Automated Program Repair"), and [19] ("Diffusion is a code repair operator and generator") all operate in the general area of program repair behavior analysis. For example, [3] analyzes intermediate signals during repair, and [19] evaluates diffusion models for last-mile code repair. These papers address repair behavior analysis broadly, even if the specific repair strategies or contexts differ.
